title: Patbingsu
subtitle: Shaved ice dessert with sweet red bean and rice cakes
excerpt: Finely shaved or crushed ice is piled into bowls and topped with sweet red bean paste, small rice cake pieces, fresh fruit and a drizzle of condensed milk. This recipe serves 4 and takes around 25 minutes if using canned beans, or 1 hour 20 minutes if cooking dried red beans from scratch. Patbingsu is Korea's most popular summer dessert.
sourceNotes: Bingsu, shaved ice dessert, has been made in Korea since the Joseon dynasty when ice was stored in ice houses called seokbinggo and distributed to the royal court. The sweet red bean topping that defines patbingsu became standard in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Modern versions now include a huge range of toppings, but the red bean remains the defining element.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sweet red bean paste can be made up to 3 days ahead and kept in the fridge. The ice must be prepared and served immediately. Assemble just before eating.

glossaryTerms.definition: Patbingsu is Korea's iconic summer shaved ice dessert, combining 'pat' (sweet red bean) and 'bingsu' (shaved ice). It is served in large bowls piled high with finely shaved ice that has a snow-like texture, topped with various sweet accompaniments. Patbingsu is so beloved in Korea that dedicated bingsu cafes are filled to capacity throughout the summer months, and the dish is considered by many Koreans to be the defining taste of summer.

Pat refers to adzuki beans cooked and sweetened into a paste or loose topping used across Korean desserts. In patbingsu, the pat is typically chunky rather than fully smooth, with some whole or half-broken beans visible in the mix. It is cooked with sugar until thick and jammy and acts as the primary flavour base for the dessert. Pat is also used in tteok rice cakes, sweet soups and other traditional Korean sweets.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes around 25 minutes using canned beans or up to 1 hour 20 minutes if cooking dried beans from scratch.
is all about the contrast between cold, airy ice and warm, sweet
. The condensed milk is optional: omit it to keep the recipe fully dairy-free and vegan, or replace with oat condensed milk for the same sweetness without the dairy.

The texture of the ice makes or breaks this dessert. A block of frozen water blended briefly in a food processor gives a reasonable coarse crush, but a dedicated shaved ice machine produces the snow-like texture of the real thing. Alternatively, freeze water in a shallow tray and scrape it with a fork to create fine ice flakes. Whatever method you use, work quickly once the ice is ready, as it melts fast.

content.text: If using dried beans: drain the soaked adzuki beans and place in a saucepan. Cover with fresh water and bring to the boil. Reduce to a simmer and cook for 45 to 60 minutes until the beans are completely tender and can be squashed easily between two fingers. Drain, reserving a little of the cooking liquid.
If using canned beans: drain and rinse them. Skip the long cooking step.

Make the sweet red bean topping. Place the cooked or canned beans in a saucepan with the sugar, a pinch of salt and 3 to 4 tablespoons of water. Cook over a medium-low heat, stirring frequently, for 10 to 15 minutes until the mixture thickens to a jammy consistency with some whole beans still visible. Set aside to cool slightly.
Cook the small tteok pieces in boiling water for 2 to 3 minutes until soft, then drain and rinse with cold water. Set aside.
Prepare the ice. Shave, crush or scrape into fine flakes and divide between 4 large bowls, piling it high.
Top each bowl generously with the sweet red bean, the tteok pieces and the sliced strawberries. Drizzle over the condensed milk if using. Serve immediately before the ice melts.

items.symptom: Red bean paste is too watery and runs into the ice immediately
items.cause: The beans were not cooked down long enough with the sugar
items.fix: Continue cooking the sweet beans over a medium heat, stirring constantly, until the mixture is thick and jammy and holds its shape on a spoon. It will firm up further as it cools.

items.symptom: Ice is in large chunks rather than fine snow-like flakes
items.cause: The ice was not processed finely enough, or the wrong method was used
items.fix: For finer ice at home, freeze water in a shallow flat tray and scrape with a fork to create thin layers of ice flakes. Alternatively, use a powerful blender briefly in short pulses, stopping before it turns to water.

items.symptom: Tteok pieces are hard and chewy even after cooking
items.cause: They were not boiled for long enough, or were very cold from the fridge
items.fix: Boil the tteok pieces for at least 3 minutes in plenty of water. Rinse with cold water and taste one before using. They should be soft all the way through with a gentle chew, not dense or resistant.

content.text: Patbingsu defines Korean summers. Bingsu cafes in Seoul see enormous queues in July and August, with elaborate versions featuring matcha, injeolmi rice cake dust, fresh mango or premium red bean taking the place of the simple home version. The home version here is deliberately straightforward: good shaved ice, proper sweet red bean cooked from scratch or canned, fresh fruit and small rice cake pieces. It requires no specialist equipment beyond a way to produce fine ice. Make it the moment summer arrives.
